cue: Walk. The picture holds still, then lurches forward, the way a heron’s head does.
rows: Herons, egrets, cranes, pigeons and chickens hold their heads still while they walk, so their eyes stay fixed on the world. Then the head darts forward to catch up with the body. This view does the same while you walk.
In pigeons, each dart forward takes about a tenth of a second.
Most birds see half as much detail as people do, or less.

A whooping crane’s shortest-wave cone peaks near 405 nanometers and a pigeon’s near 410, both in the violet. The gene for that cone is the violet type in a gray heron, a glossy ibis and several sandpipers too, so you very likely see little ultraviolet. A starling’s same cone peaks near 360, well into the ultraviolet.
Eyes on the sides of the head probably give a wide view. This part of the view is a guess.

fov.note: the black-crowned night heron's field across the horizon, both eyes together

cpd.note: a pigeon's peak on its frontal axis, standing in for an unmeasured wader Graded i by hand: the figure is a pigeon's, from another order, and the carry rules let acuity and flicker travel only within a genus.

M.note: four cone classes from the whooping crane

rate.note: 60 hertz divided by a pigeon's 77 hertz flicker fusion Graded i by hand: the figure is a pigeon's, from another order, and the carry rules let acuity and flicker travel only within a genus.

hold.note: how long the head rests between thrusts, by analogy with a walking crane

thrust.note: the quick forward move of the head, by analogy with a walking crane

blindAt.note: the direction of the blind wedge, behind the head

blindDeg.note: 360 degrees minus the night heron's 320 degree field

rows: If you are a black-crowned night heron, each of your eyes covers about 171 degrees, and together they take in about 320 degrees across the horizon. Other herons have eyes of much the same width, about 170 degrees each.
If you are a heron, you very likely have a blind wedge of about 40 degrees directly behind your head. That figure comes from taking the night heron's 320 degree field away from a full circle.

If you are a black-crowned night heron, your two eyes overlap in a strip about 22 degrees wide that runs long from top to bottom. In three heron species, eye movements can remove this overlap at every height in front of you.

If you are a whooping crane, you have four kinds of color-sensing cones that peak at 404, 450, 499 and 561 nanometers, one more than a human, and the first responds to violet light. A gray heron's eye lets less than half the light through below about 380 nanometers, so little ultraviolet reaches the back of the eye.

If you are a whooping crane walking, you hold your head still for about 30 percent or more of each step cycle, then thrust it forward at about two hock lengths a second. When you run to food, you do not bob your head at all.
Nobody has measured how sharp a heron, a crane or an ibis sees. A pigeon reads about 11 cycles per degree along its front axis, and you very likely see in about that range.
Nobody has tested a wader for flicker. A pigeon fuses flicker at about 77 hertz in bright light, so you very likely see movement a little finer than a human does at 60 hertz.

Nobody has measured exactly where a heron's blind wedge lies, or how long and how fast a crane's head holds and thrusts as one move. Nobody has measured the color cells of a heron, an ibis or a stork either, so the whooping crane's four peaks stand in for every wader. These parts are guesses.

rows.title: Head movement
rows.text: If you are a gray heron, a little egret or a sandhill crane, you hold your head still while you walk, so your eyes stay fixed on the world. Then your head darts forward to catch up with your body, in time with your steps. Nobody has measured this in a great blue heron, a great egret or a green heron.
rows.note: Fujita 2003 filmed one bob per step in wild herons and egrets, holding during single support and thrusting during double support; Cronin 2007 found the crane's head-bobbing tied to the stepping cycle. The tick bird and the 320 degrees are cut.
rows.rewrite_reason: Draft calls the cattle egret 'tick bird' (an oxpecker's name) and repeats Field of view's 320 degrees. Recast live's hold-then-dart picture in 'you'.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A review lists a rock pigeon seeing a light flicker at about 75 flashes a second and a chicken at about 85, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. If you are a heron, egret, crane or another wading bird, nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing the flicker.
rows.note: No record covers herons, egrets, cranes or other waders; only rock pigeon (75 Hz) and chicken (87 Hz) are measured, both read from a review (Boström 2016). Replaced "reports" with "lists" and dropped the unsupported ground-feeding remark.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a heron, egret or crane, nobody has measured how sharply you see, or how closely spaced the light-sensing cells in your eye are. Two doves have a figure: a compilation lists a rock pigeon at about 12 cycles a degree in behavior tests, and a table lists a mourning dove at about 7, estimated from cell counts in its retina. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree, and those two figures belong to those two doves alone.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". No record gives acuity or receptor spacing for any heron, egret or crane, so the row stays at i.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Nobody has measured whether a heron, egret or coot senses ultraviolet, the light just beyond violet. If you are a rock pigeon, your violet-sensing cells absorb most strongly at about 410 nanometers, and in a whooping crane the same kind of pigment, made in a laboratory, absorbs most at about 405. Nobody has measured how much ultraviolet passes through the front of the eye to those cells in any of these birds.
rows.note: No record for herons, egrets or coots; peafowl and quail transmission figures left out because numbers do not travel to other genera.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: If you are a black-crowned night heron, you see about 320 degrees around your head at once, and if you are a common moorhen, about 300 degrees, with a blind area directly behind you. Both of your eyes see the same thing only in a narrow, upright strip in front of you, about 20 degrees wide in the night heron and about 35 degrees wide in the moorhen. Nobody has measured how wide a field most other waders see, including the great blue heron.
rows.note: Left out the pigeon and the cattle egret figures to keep the row short; the pigeon's 316 degrees comes from an unlabeled table column.
